title: AI Can Help Governments Help Citizens
gist: Kalpana Kochhar argues that in developing economies the binding constraint on AI's benefits is not access but state capacity; AI tools must be built to work inside government, backed by leadership, skilled civil servants and integrated digital public infrastructure, citing Maharashtra's MahaVISTAAR and Pakistan's Punjab.

insights.claim: The World Bank's World Development Report 2026 estimates that AI's productivity benefits could be more than twice as large in advanced economies as in low- and middle-income countries if current trends continue.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: AI could widen the growth gap between advanced and developing economies, affecting EM long-run growth assumptions.
insights.quote: the World Bank’s World Development Report 2026 estimates that AI’s productivity benefits could be more than twice as large in advanced economies if current trends continue

insights.claim: For low- and middle-income countries, AI could be a great equalizer or could deepen inequality, depending on decisions developers, investors and governments make now about how it is built, funded and deployed.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: Investor allocation choices in EM AI are framed as path-determining.

insights.claim: IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said at the October 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings that AI adoption depends on electricity access, digital connectivity and appropriately skilled workers.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: Power and connectivity buildout remain prerequisites for EM AI adoption—relevant for energy and telecom investment.

themes.theme: State capacity as the binding constraint

insights.claim: Kalpana Kochhar argues that access to AI, while a legitimate concern, is not the biggest barrier in developing economies; the binding constraint is the state capacity to put AI tools to use.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: EM AI plays that ignore government implementation capacity may underdeliver.
insights.quote: access, while a legitimate concern, is not the biggest barrier. Above all, AI adoption requires building the state capacity to put these tools to use

insights.claim: In developing economies, the AI debate focuses less on safety, job displacement and frontier risk than on ensuring AI tools work in local languages, train on local data and fit local realities.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: Demand exists for localized, low-resource-language AI products in emerging markets.
insights.quote: They must work in local languages, train on local data, and be built for local realities.

insights.claim: AI tools intended to serve citizens must be built to run on public systems and data, comply with countries' chosen data-sharing and security protocols, and be affordable enough for governments to procure and sustain.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: GovTech vendors must design for public-sector procurement constraints and affordability to win EM contracts.
insights.quote: AI tools intended to serve citizens must work within government, not merely be adapted to it.
insights.locator: AI tools intended to serve citizens

insights.claim: Maharashtra's MahaVISTAAR, a free AI advisory service letting farmers ask about crops, weather and pests in their own language via app, voice call or chat, has over 740,000 farmers enrolled and adds about 70,000 new users a month.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: Shows scalable demand for vernacular AI agricultural advisory in India.
insights.quote: more than 740,000 farmers have joined, with 70,000 new users signing up each month
insights.locator: But even the best-built tools will struggle

insights.claim: MahaVISTAAR costs the Maharashtra government less than 18 cents per farmer, a fraction of the cost of reaching farmers in person.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: Unit economics of AI-delivered public services can be dramatically lower than in-person delivery.
insights.quote: at a cost to the government of less than 18 cents per farmer
insights.locator: But even the best-built tools will struggle

insights.claim: MahaVISTAAR succeeded because the government treated it as a new layer of public infrastructure built on its existing farmer-advisory network rather than as a one-off app.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: Integration into existing public programs is the success factor to screen for in GovTech AI deployments.
insights.quote: The tool worked because the government viewed it as a new layer of public infrastructure built on its network for advising farmers, rather than a one-off app.
insights.locator: But even the best-built tools will struggle

insights.claim: Pakistan's Punjab province has set up a government office dedicated to AI and is working with local researchers on public-health applications, including local-language tools helping frontline workers reach mothers.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: Sub-national governments in South Asia are emerging as early AI adopters.
insights.locator: On a recent visit to Pakistan

themes.theme: Three pillars of government AI capacity

insights.claim: Kochhar's first pillar for AI capacity is leadership able to identify use cases, with institutional ownership, cross-ministry coordination, a clear budget and timelines, and a mechanism making decisions binding across agencies to avoid duplicative parallel projects.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: Countries with centralized, budgeted AI strategies are more likely to deliver; fragmented ones risk wasted spend.

insights.claim: The second pillar is civil servants with enough AI expertise to commission, acquire, integrate, evaluate and regulate AI systems, requiring talent pipelines for technical skills distinct from general digital literacy—a gap not even wealthy countries have solved.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: Public-sector AI talent shortage is a global bottleneck and an opportunity for training/advisory providers.

insights.claim: The third pillar is integrated digital public infrastructure—e-government service delivery, digital ID, payments and a secure data exchange layer—because weak digitization and fragmented vertical systems directly constrain AI performance and safety.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: Countries with mature DPI (digital ID, payments) are better positioned to capture AI gains.
insights.quote: Weak digitization and fragmented vertical systems are a direct constraint on AI performance and safety.

insights.claim: Once digital public infrastructure is in place, AI can in turn make government systems more secure by detecting fraud, cyberattacks and anomalous patterns.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: A virtuous cycle between DPI and AI security creates demand for public-sector fraud and cyber analytics.

insights.claim: Kochhar concludes that whether AI reaches underserved citizens will depend less on the pace of technology than on choices governments make now.
insights.speaker: KALPANA KOCHHAR
insights.so_what: Policy execution, not model capability, is the key variable for EM AI impact.
insights.quote: Building the tools may be the more straightforward part.
